newsitem.title: USA: Dornan opponent said set to claim victory.
newsitem.headline: Dornan opponent said set to claim victory.

text.p: Eight days after voters went to the polls, Democratic challenger Loretta Sanchez was ready to claim victory Wednesday over archconservative incumbent Republican Congressman Robert Dornan in the race for his House seat, Sanchez campaign officials said.

The officials contended the political newcomer had built an insurmountable lead, moving 929 votes ahead of her fiery conservative opponent with only a few thousand absentee ballots and so-called "provisional" votes left to be counted.
Dornan, seeking election to a 10th term in the House of Representatives, did not concede and was reportedly charging that Sanchez was helped by voter fraud.

Dornan told the Los Angeles Times that Sanchez, a well-funded Hispanic businesswoman, "ran a dirty campaign" and that he suspected large numbers of non-citizens voted. He called on the House Oversight Committee to investigate.
Wylie Aitken, Sanchez' campaign chairman, rejected the allegations, calling Dornan's charges "sad and pathetic."

As of Tuesday night Sanchez was leading with 46,270 votes to Dornan's 45,341. The voter registar's office reported about 1,000 absentee ballots remained to be counted in the race in the 46th Congressional District, which represents parts of Orange County, a traditional Republican stronghold south of Los Angeles.

In addition, 2,500 to 3,000 provisional ballots were still to be tallied, Aitken said. These required special validation because they were cast by people who changed their address and showed up to vote where they were not listed on the rolls or claimed to have lost their absentee ballots when they went to the voting booths.
"The mathematics are completely against Mr. Dornan," Aitken said. "There's no reason for our candidate not to accept the fact that she's been elected."
Sanchez, who had trailed Dornan by a slim 200-vote margin on election night, planned to claim victory at a news conference Wednesday, Aitken said.

Dornan, a former Air Force pilot known as "B-1 Bob" for his uncompromising support for the military, gained a reputation for his opposition to abortion, communism, gay rights and gun control during his 18 years in Congress. He was one of President Clinton's most outspoken critics.

During the campaign, Sanchez, a 36-year-old financial analyst, presented herself as a moderate while painting Dornan as an extremist out of step with the needs of his largely working-class constituents.
Dornan ran an unsuccessful campaign for the Republican presidential nomination earlier this year.
